title: Audit, price and win your first Google Ads clients

say: Audit, price and win your first Google Ads clients.
This is the video for module 3 of Paid Advertising with Google Ads.
Most businesses that call you have already tried ads. Before you promise anything, you need the business facts and an honest look at their account.

panel.heading: Skill pays when you win clients
items: Ask the right questions before promising
Prove your work with real evidence

say: Then you price from the real work, and you show proof of what you can do. That is how practice campaigns turn into paid work.

panel.heading: Skill pays when you win clients
items: Ask the right questions before promising
Prove your work with real evidence

say: On the discovery call, first ask what an average sale is worth and the margin they keep. Then ask how many of 10 enquiries pay, and who answers calls and WhatsApp, and how fast.

panel.heading: Six areas to ask about
items: Sales: how many of 10 enquiries pay?
Customer: what do they type, from where?
Offer: why choose you over the next ad?
History: what was tried and what it cost
Capacity: how many new jobs a month?

say: Ask what customers type when looking for them, and where they come from. And ask why someone should choose them over the next three ads.

panel.heading: Six areas to ask about
items: Sales: how many of 10 enquiries pay?
Customer: what do they type, from where?
Offer: why choose you over the next ad?
History: what was tried and what it cost
Capacity: how many new jobs a month?

say: Ask what advertising they tried and what happened. Finally, ask about capacity. If a caterer can only do four events a month and three are booked, a big campaign creates angry customers, not profit.

say: Ask for Read only access through your manager account, then audit in a fixed order. First, tracking. Do reported conversions match the client's own records?

panel.heading: Audit an account in this order

say: Second, search terms. What share of spend went to irrelevant searches in the last 30 days?

panel.heading: Audit an account in this order

say: Third, structure. Look for huge ad groups, or broad match running without reliable tracking.

panel.heading: Audit an account in this order

say: Fourth, ads and pages. Do ads match their ad groups? Are pages slow on mobile?

panel.heading: Audit an account in this order

say: Fifth, budget and bidding.

For example, Chika's furniture account reported a cost per conversion of about 2,143 naira. But it counted visits to the Contact page. Against her own log, each real lead cost about 12,857 naira. So fix measurement first.

panel.heading: Audit an account in this order
panel.rule: Fix measurement first. Every other number rests on it.

say: Remember there are two costs. Ad spend goes from the client to Google. Your management fee pays for your time and skill.
A flat monthly fee is easy to budget for and does not reward overspending, but review it if the work grows.

panel.heading: Flat fee or percentage of spend?
right: Can look like a push to spend

say: A percentage of spend grows with the account, but small budgets give tiny fees, and it can look like a reason to spend more. Many freelancers use a setup fee plus a flat monthly fee.

panel.heading: Flat fee or percentage of spend?
right: Can look like a push to spend

say: Amaka is pricing an events company in Lagos that plans 600,000 naira a month in ads. Her working rate is 12,000 naira an hour.
Setup takes 16 hours: discovery, tracking, research, build and checks. That is 192,000 naira, so she quotes 200,000.
Each month takes about 10 hours of optimisation, testing and reporting. That is 120,000 naira a month.
A 15% fee would be only 90,000 naira, which would not cover her hours. So she offers the flat fee, reviewed after 3 months or if ad spend changes by more than half.
Three money rules protect you both. First, keep spend and fee separate, and say so in writing.

cards.d: Say it plainly: your ad budget goes to Google. My fee is for managing it.
Setup fee before you begin, monthly fees at the start of each month, with an invoice each time.
No promised positions, leads or cost per lead before the account has data.

say: Second, ask for the setup fee before you begin and monthly fees in advance. Issue an invoice each time, and keep copies for your records and tax.

cards.d: Say it plainly: your ad budget goes to Google. My fee is for managing it.
Setup fee before you begin, monthly fees at the start of each month, with an invoice each time.
No promised positions, leads or cost per lead before the account has data.

say: Third, never guarantee positions, leads or a cost per lead before the account has data. The first 30 days are for proving tracking, finding keywords that convert and cutting waste.

cards.d: Say it plainly: your ad budget goes to Google. My fee is for managing it.
Setup fee before you begin, monthly fees at the start of each month, with an invoice each time.
No promised positions, leads or cost per lead before the account has data.

say: Your proposal names the goal and how it is measured, what is included, and what is not, like landing page design. It lists client duties, such as answering leads promptly. It gives a timeline with a first review at 30 days, plus payment and exit terms.
Anything outside scope gets a short written quote before you start.

panel.heading: What the proposal must say
items: Goal and how it is measured

say: To remember. Ask about economics, sales and capacity first. Audit tracking before anything else. Price from honest hours times your rate. Keep ad spend and your fee separate.
And build proof honestly: a small real campaign or a labelled sample build, with Google Ads Search and Measurement certificates from Skillshop.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Ask about economics, sales and capacity first
Price from honest hours times your rate
Ad spend and your fee are separate
Label samples and practice work honestly

say: Your tasks: run a 20-minute practice discovery call, price and scope one client in a one-page proposal, and write your 90-day plan.
